subject: National monitoring of species using occupancy models

messages.author: cf45c6aa992bbacc
messages.subject: National monitoring of species using occupancy models
parts:
Hi,

A long-term mammal monitoring programme will begin in Spain in the coming year. The goal is to generate national-scale distribution probability maps for each species using hierarchical models and data from detection-non-detection sampling. It is a long-distance race, and we are still brainstorming about the survey protocols (repeated surveys, multiple observers, etc.) and modelling framework (static/dynamic occupancy models, integrated models if different data sources are necessary/advisable, etc.).

We know that occupancy models were used in Switzerland for the Swiss Breeding Bird Atlas. Are you aware of other large-scale (state/national) monitoring projects using hierarchical models to account for imperfect detectability? Any assistance or suggestions would be greatly appreciated!
Best,

Simone

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] National monitoring of species using occupancy models
parts:
Dear Simone,

we use occupancy models also for our annually updated trend models for about 60 middle-common to rare species in Switzerland.

I know that it may be more expensive to collect data such that one can explicitly model false-negative measurement errors, but I would suggest to any new scheme to collect such extra information at the very least for some subset of the program. For instance, in a proportion of sites or every other year.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] National monitoring of species using occupancy models
parts:
Marc, thank you very much!
The information in the Methods chapter of the Swiss Breeding Bird Atlas proved useful. Monitoring programs for mammals and birds differ significantly. We will most likely rely primarily on track surveys and camera trapping, and we are attempting to determine how a sampling design for mammals in a country the size of Spain should be. Of course, if anyone has any additional suggestions or hints, it would be greatly appreciated!

messages.author: e294dd6d325c0bfa
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] National monitoring of species using occupancy models
parts:
Simone,
 It is not quite the question you asked, but it is perhaps worth noticing that mammals (at least certain species) can be counted on bird transects, at least here in the UK 
https://www.bto.org/our-science/projects/breeding-bird-survey/latest-results/mammal-monitoring
 We don't routinely analyse them in a hierarchical way (although I guess we could), but maybe a similar thing could provide an (additional?) data source for you at relatively low cost?
 Good luck with your project, it sounds very valuable :)
Cheers
Rob

messages.author: 247b990d236a7af6
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] National monitoring of species using occupancy models
parts:
Simone, this is another "not quite the question you asked" response.

We have monitored Marbled Murrelets off the coast of the western US for over 25 years using "distance" methods to account for lack of perfect detection:  https://www.fs.usda.gov/r6/reo/monitoring/downloads/murrelet/20211101-mciver-etal-2021-status-trend-marbled-murrelet-2000-2018-pnw-gtr996.pdf.

My most important advice for long-term monitoring (after accounting for less-than-perfect detection) is to build-in the ability to handle fluctuating resources (and even with constant budgets buying power almost always decreases).

Jim
